hints: Remember which subatomic particle controls the identity of an element and must stay the same, and which particle changes the mass but not the chemistry.
walkthrough:
Fix what must stay the same**
You are looking at two atoms that are both gallium, so picture the nucleus. Both must have the same atomic number, 31 protons, plus 31 electrons to be neutral. If protons changed, it would no longer be gallium.

See what changes the mass**
The mass numbers are 69 and 71. Since protons are fixed at 31, the extra mass must come from neutrons. So $^{69}\text{Ga}$ has $69-31 = 38$ neutrons and $^{71}\text{Ga}$ has $71-31 = 40$ neutrons. Different neutron number is the definition of isotopes.
Final answer: The isotopes have a different number of neutrons ($^{69}\text{Ga}$ has 38 and $^{71}\text{Ga}$ has 40).

hints: Think of $A_r$ as a weighted mean, the mass of each isotope counts according to how much of it is present.
walkthrough:
Treat $A_r$ as a weighted average**
Relative atomic mass is not just the average of 69 and 71. Imagine a sample with far more $^{69}\text{Ga}$ than $^{71}\text{Ga}$, the average would sit much closer to 69. To weight correctly you need to know what fraction of the atoms is each isotope, that is the relative abundance of each isotope.
Final answer: The relative abundance / percentage abundance of each isotope of gallium.

hints: At $500^{\circ}\text{C}$ gallium trichloride is a gas of separate $\text{GaCl}_3$ molecules, so think about what holds atoms together inside one molecule versus what holds separate molecules together.
Recall the strong shared electron pair attraction inside a molecule and the very weak temporary dipole attraction that is all that exists between separate simple molecules in the gas phase.
walkthrough:
Picture the gas at $500^{\circ}\text{C}$**
You have individual $\text{GaCl}_3$ molecules flying around freely. That tells you the structure is simple molecular. The atoms inside each molecule are joined by strong shared pairs of electrons.

Name the strong attraction inside**
Gallium and chlorine share electrons to form $\text{Ga-Cl}$ bonds. These are covalent bonds, strong attractions between nuclei and shared electron pairs within the molecule. They are not broken when the solid boils to a gas.

Name the weak attraction between**
Between one $\text{GaCl}_3$ molecule and the next there is no sharing, only fleeting uneven electron distributions creating temporary dipoles. These London dispersion, also called induced dipole-dipole, forces are very weak, which is why little energy is needed to separate the molecules into a gas.

Final answer: between atoms within a gallium trichloride molecule: covalent bonds.
between gallium trichloride molecules: London dispersion / induced dipole-dipole forces.

hints: Think of aluminium chloride dimer, $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$, where a lone pair on chlorine on one molecule is donated into the empty orbital on the Group 13 metal of another.
walkthrough:
Link to aluminium behaviour**
Gallium is below aluminium in Group 13, so $\text{GaCl}_3$ is electron deficient with only six electrons around Ga. Just like $\text{AlCl}_3$ forms $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$, two $\text{GaCl}_3$ units join together on cooling.

See how the bridge forms**
A lone pair on a chlorine atom of one $\text{GaCl}_3$ is donated into the empty p orbital on the gallium of the other. Because both electrons in the new $\text{Ga-Cl}$ bridge come from chlorine, this is a coordinate, also called dative covalent, bond.

hints: Gallium is in Group 13 like aluminium, so work out the charge on the gallium ion and the formula of its oxide with $\text{O}^{2-}$.
Start your equation from $\text{Ga} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow$ oxide product and balance Ga and O atoms.
walkthrough:
Work out the oxide formula**
Group 13 metals lose three electrons to form $\text{Ga}^{3+}$. With oxide ions, $\text{O}^{2-}$, you need two $\text{Ga}^{3+}$ and three $\text{O}^{2-}$ to balance charges, giving $\text{Ga}_2\text{O}_3$. This is exactly analogous to $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$. The white solid layer is this oxide.

Balance the reaction with oxygen**
Write the skeleton: $$\text{Ga} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ga}_2\text{O}_3$$ To get 6 O atoms on each side you need $3\text{O}_2$ and $2\text{Ga}_2\text{O}_3$, which then needs $4\text{Ga}$. Check: 4 Ga and 6 O on both sides: $$4\text{Ga} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Ga}_2\text{O}_3$$

hints: Look at the table, the same oxide forms a salt with hydrochloric acid and also forms a gallate with sodium hydroxide, so what word describes an oxide that reacts with both?
walkthrough:
Read what the products tell you**
With hot aqueous $\text{HCl}$ the oxide gives $\text{GaCl}_3$, normal basic oxide behaviour forming a salt plus water. With hot aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ it gives $\text{NaGa(OH)}_4$, normal acidic oxide behaviour forming a complex anion.

Give the key term**
An oxide that can act as both a base toward acids and an acid toward bases is amphoteric. This matches aluminium oxide, confirming the similarity between aluminium and gallium compounds.
